title: Vessantara, read whole
hook: the generous prince's tale, read from the white elephant to the homecoming (Jataka 547)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the clever sage, panna itself. Your line was wit that saves. This week brought a king shown heaven and hell, a prince saved by truth, a serpent who kept his vows, a daughter who argued, a minister who taught his captor, and that clever sage. Today, the tale they lead to. Day eight hundred forty-seven.

The elephant is white, and the people of the Sivi kingdom say it brings the rain. One morning, envoys arrive from Kalinga, a land dried out by drought, and they ask the crown prince for it. The prince pours water over their hands to seal the gift and hands the elephant over. By evening the city is furious, and the king is pressed to send his own son into exile. The prince is Vessantara. Tradition places his tale at the end of the Jataka and tells it as the bodhisatta's last life before the one in which he became the Buddha. Today we read it whole.
screen: `A WHITE ELEPHANT, GIVEN AWAY.` → `A CITY IN UPROAR.` → `A PRINCE SENT INTO EXILE.`

segments.voice: First, the road out. Vessantara leaves with his wife Maddi and their two small children, Jali and Kanhajina. He gives away his wealth before he goes, and on the road he gives away the chariot and the horses too, so the family walks. They settle in huts on a mountain called Vankagiri and live simply. Second, the hardest gift. An old brahmin named Jujaka, pushed by a young wife who wants servants, finds the hermitage while Maddi is out gathering fruit, and he asks for the children. Vessantara gives them. What Maddi finds when she comes home belongs to tomorrow, so we leave that scene for now. Third, the last test. The god Sakka arrives disguised as a brahmin and asks for Maddi herself. Vessantara gives her too, and Sakka at once gives her back and shows who he is. Fourth, the homecoming. Jujaka leads the children to their grandfather, the king, who ransoms them. The whole court goes up the mountain, the family is together again, and Vessantara returns as king. In the telling, the earth shakes at his gifts. This is a hard tale, and Buddhists have said so themselves. In the Questions of King Milinda, a king asks the monk Nagasena about it directly: was giving away the children not cruel? Nagasena answers by calling it a gift almost too great to do, made for the sake of awakening. Some readers hear in it dana, generosity, carried to its very edge. Others point out that the tale itself never hides the cost: the children's fear and the mother's grief are told in full. Read in pieces, it can sound like a parable about letting go. Read whole, it holds the gift and what the gift costs, and it ends with everyone home.
screen: `THE ROAD OUT, ON FOOT.` · `THE HARDEST GIFT.` · `SAKKA ASKS FOR MADDI.` · `THE FAMILY HOME AGAIN.` · then, large: `THE GIFT AND WHAT IT COSTS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: read one scene aloud. Pick a moment from today's tale: the white elephant handed over, the family walking without a chariot, the god giving Maddi back, the reunion on the mountain. Tell it out loud in your own words, slowly, in a few sentences, as if to a child at bedtime. Notice which scene you chose, and which ones you passed over. Then let the story go quiet and rest with the breath. The bell holds the time.
Vessantara. The prince who gave away everything he was asked for, told as the bodhisatta's last life before the Buddha. Today's word.
Your line: the last life. Today, when you give something, time or money or attention, notice what it costs you, and let that part be seen too. Day eight hundred forty-seven.

howItsDone: In Theravada lands the Vessantara tale is retold, chanted and painted, and some communities recite it in full at a yearly festival as a teaching on generosity.

fork.setup: you're the crown prince. envoys from a land in drought ask for the white elephant your people believe brings the rain. what do you do?
options: refuse. the kingdom needs its rain too.
fork.reveal: he gives it, sealing the gift with water poured over their hands. his own city is so angry that he is sent into exile.

original.note: Pali: dakkhinodaka, the water poured over the hands to seal a gift, as Vessantara does with the white elephant.

trapdoor: what you thought: a story about a man who gave his family away.
what it means: a tale of generosity pushed to its limit, which tells the cost in full and ends with everyone home.
what a scholar hears: the Questions of King Milinda treats the gift of the children as a hard question; the tale is placed at the end of the Jataka as the bodhisatta's last life before the Buddha.

sources.ref: Milindapanha, the dilemma of Vessantara's gifts

notes: 'The bodhisatta's last life before the one in which he became the Buddha': tradition places a heavenly life in Tusita between Vessantara and Siddhattha; the script says 'last life' per the index carry. Keeper may prefer 'last human life'.

Confirm names and details: Jali and Kanhajina; Vankagiri; Jujaka sent by his young wife; Sakka disguised as a brahmin asking for Maddi; grandfather King Sanjaya ransoming the children; earth shaking at the gifts.

Milindapanha: Nagasena's answer is summarized very briefly ('a gift almost too great to do, made for the sake of awakening'). Confirm it is fair; his fuller answer includes Vessantara's knowledge that the grandfather would ransom the children.
howItsDone: festival recitation (e.g. Thet Mahachat in Thailand, Bun Phawet in Laos) stated generally as 'some communities'; confirm.
